reason: The intro says muscle precursors join into long cells, and the fusion proteins are pictured between those precursors.
expectation: The precursor cells should join into a fibre with multiple nuclei.

effect: The precursors formed one long, many-nucleated fibre with actin and myosin, but their grip sites are still covered.
reaction: It is interesting that one muscle fibre is a single cell with many nuclei.
reason: The calcium signal spreads around the fibre's filaments, so it seems like the next step toward making them pull.
expectation: Calcium should let the filaments interact and make the fibre pull.

effect: Calcium uncovered grip sites, allowing the filaments to slide and the fibre to shorten. It still needs to become ready again.
reaction: It is surprising that the fibre shortens without the filaments themselves shortening.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes have pumps and ATP, suggesting they can move calcium back into storage.
expectation: Calcium should return to storage so the fibre can relax and be ready again.

effect: The calcium pumps returned calcium to storage, stopping the pull and leaving the fibre ready again. The next goal is to build both arm muscles.
reaction: I didn't expect relaxation to need ATP too.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces, so the relaxed fibre seems like a suitable piece to put into them.
expectation: The fibre should fit into the biceps sheaths to help build the muscle.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs fibres, but either muscle seems reasonable to start with.

effect: The fibre needed collagen-rich matrix first, forming bundles called fascicles with enough for both muscles.
reaction: I hadn't realized the connective layers had to come before the muscle sheaths.
reason: The fascicles are bundles of muscle fibres, and the biceps sheaths have spaces for muscle tissue.
expectation: The fascicles should fill the biceps sheaths to build the muscle.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs bundles, so it could be built first instead.

effect: The fascicles filled the biceps sheaths, connecting the muscle fibres to its tendons. The triceps still needs to be built.
reaction: The force path from fibres through connective tissue to tendon makes the layers clearer.
reason: The fascicles were described as enough for both muscles, and the triceps sheaths also have empty muscle-head spaces.
expectation: The remaining fascicles should fill the triceps sheaths and form the muscle with its tendons.

effect: The triceps is now built with its tendons; both muscles still need attachment across the elbow.
reaction: The picture makes the three triceps heads and their shared tendon clearer.
reason: The biceps tendons lead toward the shoulder and radius, so attaching them to the arm skeleton should advance the goal.
expectation: The biceps should attach across the elbow on the arm skeleton.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs attachment, so it could be tried first.

effect: The biceps is attached across the elbow, and the arm assembly has an empty extensor slot for the opposing muscle.
reaction: The poses clarify how the biceps pulls the forearm to bend the elbow.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle, and its tendon reaches the ulna on the opposite side of the elbow.
expectation: The triceps should fill the extensor slot and attach across the elbow.

effect: The triceps filled the remaining slot, completing the arm assembly. Its attachment makes its pull straighten the elbow, opposite to the biceps' bending action.
reaction: Seeing how similar pulls produce opposite movements made the muscle attachments feel meaningful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Attaching the two muscles was most worthwhile: their positions helped explain how one bends the elbow and the other straightens it.

leastWorthwhile.text: Trying to put the fibre directly into the biceps sheath was initially confusing because I hadn't understood that it needed connective layers first. The feedback did move the construction forward.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the fibre shortens by filaments sliding past each other, rather than the filaments shortening.

arbitrary.text: The matrix-before-sheath prerequisite wasn't obvious to me when I tried it, although the resulting picture explained the connective layers around the bundles.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: connecting the small-scale sliding mechanism to the arm's movement made me curious about how another body system works.
